title: The Hokkaido Birth Cohort Study on Environment and Children's Health: cohort profile-updated 2017.
ehr_evidence: Parent and infant medical records were obtained from physicians at the participating hospitals or clinics.
summary: Cohort profile of the Hokkaido Birth Cohort Study on Environment and Children’s Health, detailing two prospective cohorts investigating prenatal environmental chemical exposures on birth outcomes, child development, allergies, and epigenetic modifications.
key_findings: PCDD/PCDFs significantly decreased birth weight (2,3,4,7,8-PeCDF: β = −24.5 g, 95% CI −387.4 to −61.5).
PFOS was negatively correlated with birth weight (per log10 unit: β = −269.4 g, 95% CI −465.7 to −73.0).
PFOA was negatively associated with ponderal index (per log10 unit: β = −0.73 kg/m3, 95% CI −1.44 to −0.02).
DEHP significantly decreased ponderal index (per log10 unit: β = −1.28, 95% CI −2.43 to −0.13).
PFOA was negatively associated with mental development in 6-month-old girls (per log10 unit: β = −0.296, 95% CI −11.96 to −0.682).
Polychlorinated dibenzofuran was associated with increased risk of otitis media in male infants (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.1–5.9).
PFTrDA decreased the risk of eczema at 24 months (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.86).
PFOS was associated with reduced cortisol and cortisone levels in cord blood (Q4 vs Q1: β = −23.98 ng/mL, 95% CI −47.12 to −11.99).
Prenatal PFOA exposure was significantly inversely associated with IGF2 methylation, mediating reduced ponderal index.
captured_features: environmental chemical concentrations (blood, hair, milk, dust, urine)
study_design: prospective birth cohort study with nested case-cohort design
population: pregnant women and their offspring in Hokkaido, Japan (Sapporo cohort n=514, Hokkaido cohort n=20,926), followed from pregnancy through childhood
exposure_domain: environmental chemicals (dioxins, PCBs, PFASs, organochlorine pesticides, phthalates, bisphenol A, methylmercury, tobacco smoke)
limitations: cohort profile design limits primary hypothesis testing
reliance on self-reported questionnaires for some covariates
low environmental chemical exposure levels in Japan may limit generalizability
multiple comparisons without strict correction in some analyses
